from such malpractices to ensure that the sanctity of examinations are protected. Let this examination be a celebration of hard work, not a plot on academic integrity. To our students, please trust in your preparation. You have worked hard for this. Do not jeopardise your future by attempting to cheat. To school heads and invigilators, you have a duty to uphold fairness and discipline throughout the examination period. WAEC and the Ghana Education Service must intensify supervision, sensitisation and enforcement of sanctions where necessary to safeguard the credibility of this critical academic milestone, which they are doing anyway. Mr Speaker, education is not only a personal journey, it is a constitutional right. Article 38 (2) of the 1992 71 13th June, 2025 72 Statements Constitution charges government to ensure access to free universal basic education. As such, this House must reaffirm its commitment to strengthening infrastructure and teaching resources, expanding training and ethical oversight for educators, investing in digital and inclusive education delivery and improving student support systems, especially in the era of artificial intelligence. Mr Speaker, as our sons and daughters prepare or are already writing this B.E.C.E., let us rally behind them with encouragement and unwavering support. Let us also send strong messages that malpractice has no place in our examination halls. Their success is not only personal; it is the building blocks in the foundation of the future of Ghana. I wish all candidates the very best. May their efforts be rewarded with success and may they continue to raise their honesty, determination and excellence. Mr Speaker, I am extremely grateful for this opportunity. The Speaker: Hon Members, can we now take comments from those who are interested in doing so? How many did we agree to take? Well, we have two Statements. Yes? Mr Dafeamekpor: Mr Speaker, my understanding is that there is another Statement from my brother, Hon Dapaah, also in respect of the B.E.C.E candidates. The Speaker: It is in respect of what? Mr Dafeamekpor: Mr Speaker, the Minority Leader had a Statement and there was an issue about it, so I want to urge him to make that prayer before you. So, before we do that, Mr Speaker, may I urge you that we take the comments on those that have been read, so that we can deal with the outstanding Statement. Mr Speaker, let me pray that we do two on each Side in respect of the two Statements. So, that will be four in all. Thank you. The Speaker: Hon Members, there is a proposal of two-two, that means two from each Side of the House. Mr Dafeamekpor: Mr Speaker, that is so, plus leadership, that will be three. The Speaker: Yes. Since the Statement came from the Member from Kintampo North, can we hear from the Minority Side? Osahen Afenyo-Markin: Mr Speaker, with respect, we are fine. They can take the two from their Side. The Speaker: So, we will take two comments from the Majority Side. Osahen Afenyo-Markin: Yes. The Speaker: That is on the Hon Member for Kintampo North, and

the Hon Minister for Education have vamoosed and are no longer captured. How can that be possible at a time like this with all the challenges we have in the educational sector? So, I am pleading with Leadership to reconsider because some of the matters are urgent and time- sensitive. I do not know the justification as to why the Questions have been admitted and advertised for the past two weeks, but in the Business Statement for the ensuing week, they have suddenly disappeared. Please, I am on my knees. This country's educational system is on the verge of a crisis and we need to rescue it— My fellow Vandal says I should kneel down. He knows what we do in Commonwealth Hall. I so submit. Mr Peter Lanchene Toobu: Thank you, Mr Speaker, for the opportunity. Let me thank Leadership for the good job done. I realised that the Hon Minister for the Interior is slated to be in the House next week to answer about six Questions. Mr Speaker, something is happening in the 53 12th July, 2024 54 Business of the House country and everybody is getting worried. There is a sound of recruitment in the air. If we go to the National Police Training School (NPTS), currently as I speak to you, there are young men and women who are there hoping to go through medical examinations, and this is the first time I have heard that the recruitment process starts with medical examination. It has never happened in history. Mr Speaker, I filed an Urgent Question, and I am surprised to look through this document and not find it. I would want clarity on whether it was not admitted or it was admitted but was found not suitable to be answered. Probably, if you can do that during the Committee of the Whole, I would appreciate it. The people of Ghana are waiting to hear something from the Hon Minister for the Interior regarding the current recruitment stories all over the media space. Mr Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa: Thank you very much, Mr Speaker. Mr Speaker, you would recall that last week after the presentation of the Business Statement, I submitted that I had taken intelligence that the Volta River Authority (VRA) would soon spill excess water from the Akosombo Dam. Later that day, in the evening, the VRA put out a statement confirming that they were about to spill excess water. Indeed, they have begun stakeholder consultations in our communities to prepare the minds of those of us who live near the dam to get ready for another spillage. Mr Speaker, it is with a heavy heart that I remind you and this House that it has been 10 good months since the September 15th spillage, which unleashed untold disaster and devastation. More than 60,000 people were displaced. In my constituency, there were more than 12,000 people that were displaced. Ten months ago, we filed a Motion, and the Speaker assured us that there would be a Committee of enquiry so that, most importantly, we learn lessons.

Can I give you an opportunity to come back with a Statement later on education because I am very much interested in this matter? Dr Adutwum: Mr Speaker, the Statement said that there is a decline in the quality, and Ghanaians are watching us. My Hon Colleague asked a question on the change in curriculum. The curriculum has been changed. So many different things are happening now. There has been a change in curriculum, and it is the implementation of that curriculum that is leading to the improvements that we are seeing in a number of schools across the country. Mr Speaker, the literacy rate of this country, which was at a point in time two per cent for primary two students in terms of proficiency, has risen to 38 per cent. We are not where we need to be — Mr Speaker: Proficiency in what? Dr Adutwum: Reading in primary two. Mr Speaker: Reading what? Dr Adutwum: Reading. Literacy. Mr Speaker: English or Twi? Dr Adutwum: English. Mr Speaker: Is that our language? It is one of the challenges they have pointed out. We do not develop any society using another society’s language. It is something we have to look at. Please, maybe, you will need to take the Official Report, go through it and come up with a comprehensive Statement, because we are the leaders. The political leaders are here. We are those who work on the manifestoes of the various political parties. If we see that there is a problem with our educational system, we have to lead and make sure that it changes. We will all agree in this country that corruption is systemic, and so the best way of solving corruption is to change the system. We are not prepared to change that system, but we keep on blaming each other. We are talking about education, and we know the problem. Nation building is a joint effort. We have formal and informal education. Most of the contributions are based on the formal. What about the informal sector? At our family and societal levels, what do we do to assist in education? Please, it is not about now or yesterday. Generally, we have seen that we have backslid. Even with the introduction of these new policies you are talking about, we are still backsliding. The type of education we are doing is, to tell you the least, not relevant to our environment as a country. Please, I think I would give you another opportunity to come with a Statement on this matter, so that we look at it again.

Mr Speaker, is it rather not fair for students to be held responsible for the negligence of WAEC, in executing its duty of ensuring examinations are conducted in a fair and transparent manner, through its invigilators and examination officers on the day of the examination. Mr Speaker, in a country where students are provided with past questions and answers as a study guide, would it not be obvious that students would have the same answers or similar answers where similar questions are put before them? In light of the foregoing, it is my candid view that it is unfair for WAEC to 131 11th February, 2025 132 Statements flag 319 schools for alleged collusion detected by examiners during script marking. The actions of WAEC led some affected candidates to mount a legal challenge in the High Court, which resulted in a ruling in their favour, and the High Court ordered WAEC to release the withheld results. Mr Speaker, as I make this statement, I believe universities have closed admissions, and both parents of the affected students are in a state of confusion, with anxiety concerning what the future holds for their children. I am pleading with the Government, Ministry of Education, and WAEC, to look into the issue holistically, and resolve it as soon as possible, to prevent any miscarriage of justice. Thank you, Mr Speaker. Dr Fred Kyei Asamoah — rose — The Speaker: Yes, Hon Member for Offinso North, are you up? Dr Asamoah: Yes, Mr Speaker. The Speaker: You may go ahead. Dr Fred Kyei Asamoah (NPP — Offinso North): Mr Speaker, thank you for the opportunity to contribute to the Statement. As the just outgone Director-General for Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET), I had the opportunity to supervise the examination of over 46,000 learners in this country for the TVET sector. Mr Speaker, examination is not a way to punish students; but it is an opportunity to verify students' competence and to encourage learning within the school environment. Many a time, what happens is that either facilitators or in other words, teachers, are not teaching, or learners are not learning. As such, within the TVET sector, we devise a means of encouraging learning, and I believe it will be continued. That is randomisation and serialisation; this, we believe, is curbing examination malpractices. But Mr Speaker, nobody likes examinations; even PhD students do not like to take it. So, examination malpractices would not be out of the system, but we can find a way to reduce it so that we improve on competence, as the learners are the ones that end up becoming practitioners. Mr Speaker, it is quite unfortunate a lot of issues came out of the Statement. One had to do with delay in releasing examination results, and the other had to do with methodology or approach of conducting examinations. The last one had to do with examination malpractices, where some students need to be interviewed or heard.
